items.title: Google Research open-sources Harness²: agents that rewrite their own execution harness mid-task
items.summary: A framework from Google Cloud AI Research and Northwestern lets an agent propose, test, and compose edits to its own harness (system prompt, tool guidance, subagents, skills) for the task at hand, then banks what worked into a reusable library. On the WorkBuddy benchmark with Gemini 3.5 Flash in OpenCode, average score goes from 72.4 to 77.5 after one improvement pass, and to 80.8 with 5-way parallel recursion. Code and paper are public.
items.why: The gap between a generic coding agent and one tuned for your repo might just be letting the agent edit its own playbook instead of you editing it for it.
items.action: Clone google-research/harness2 and run its task-level recursion step against one of your own recurring task types, see what edit it finds that you wouldn't have thought to make.

items.title: How Claude Code, OpenCode, and Pi each structure prompt caching, and what silently breaks it
items.summary: A breakdown of where each coding harness puts its cache breakpoint, and the shared rule: static content first, volatile content last, stable key per session. Break that order once and you re-pay for the whole prefix.
items.why: If you're not watching the cache-read token metric, you could be silently paying full price on every turn without knowing why.
items.action: Check whichever harness you're building on against this ordering, and watch the cache-read metric on a session where nothing should have invalidated it.

items.title: Claude solves a 25-year-old cryptography mystery: where NIST's elliptic curve seeds came from
items.summary: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team set Claude on the long-standing “are the NIST curves backdoored” question. In under 30 minutes it worked out the P-192 through P-521 seeds are outputs of the 1990s lrand48 generator seeded with Unix timestamps, not hash digests as long rumored, then used LLL lattice reduction and brute force to recover and confirm the hidden generator state. Reproducible Python is published under CC0.
items.why: This isn't a benchmark score, it's Claude running a real guess-and-verify cryptanalysis workflow on a question nobody had cracked since 1999.
items.action: Worth reading end to end as a template: point an agent at an old unsolved technical mystery in your own domain and see what a guess-and-verify loop turns up.
